idiom_name: one owning object (guard) with a private resource and a policy check in every published operation
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: put the resource inside one object, make that object's interface the only way to reach it, and let every published operation resolve the caller, consult the policy and only then touch the resource - decision and use in one call, deny when the check cannot be answered. Keep the resource out of getters, return values and constructor escapes (hand out guarded views, copies or revocable handles instead), keep the policy in a separate replaceable source so rules change without editing the guard, and keep the guard's surface as narrow as the use cases allow. Where the language or runtime can actually make the resource unreachable (module privacy, opaque handle, private fields without reflection, an OS handle), the ownership claim is enforced; where it cannot, the pattern degrades to a convention and a real boundary needs the process, kernel or container layer.
code_sketch:
guard = Guard(resource, policy)      # resource and policy are private to guard
# callers only ever see guard:
guard.read(caller, id)
# inside the guard:
def read(caller, id):
    if not policy.allows(caller, id):
        raise Denied(id)             # decided in the same call
    return resource.load(id)         # resource itself is never returned
pitfalls: Handing the raw resource out once - through a getter, a return value, a copy or a leaky iterator - re-opens every path the guard was built to close.
Relying on language-level privacy alone as the security boundary while reflection, unsafe code or a foreign-function interface can reach the resource.
Letting the guard accumulate business logic and one method per call site until it is too large to review and its policy is untestable.
Treating an unavailable policy source or a missing identity as permission instead of denying.

Adding a checked facade while leaving another raw handle, endpoint or administrative path reachable: the alternate path bypasses the guard; instead make the guard the sole owner and mediate every entry point.

Caching an allow decision beyond authority revocation: stale permission survives the policy change; instead bound cache lifetime and invalidate it on revocation, or check the current policy per operation.

Calling an in-process wrapper a tamper-proof reference monitor: same-process code can bypass or modify it; instead move enforcement to a kernel, sandbox or separate service when that threat is in scope.
